meta.title: Who really said "Hope is itself a species of happiness, and, perhaps, the chief happiness which this world affords"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — Samuel Johnson wrote it, in a letter of 8 June 1762 printed in Boswell's Life of Johnson. Not from The Idler, as often claimed.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Hope is itself a species of happiness, and, perhaps, the chief happiness which this world affords'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Samuel Johnson — from his 8 June 1762 letter recorded in Boswell's Life of Johnson (1791), not The Idler No. 58 as often cited.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Johnson wrote this in a letter of 8 June 1762, gently declining a lady’s request that he solicit the Archbishop of Canterbury’s patronage for her son. James Boswell printed the letter in his Life of Samuel Johnson (1791), where the exact wording is confirmed. It is often mis-cited to The Idler No. 58, which carries a similar thought in different words.

docMeta.dd: The Life of Samuel Johnson, LL.D. (1791)

source.excerpt: Hope is itself a species of happiness, and, perhaps, the chief happiness which this world affords: but, like all other pleasures immoderately enjoyed, the excesses of hope must be expiated by pain; and expectations improperly indulged, must end in disappointment.
trail: The exact wording comes from a letter Johnson wrote on 8 June 1762, printed in Boswell’s Life of Johnson, under the year 1762 ↗.
Wikiquote lists the line in its sourced section, citing this same 8 June 1762 letter ↗.
It is not from The Idler No. 58 (26 May 1759), where Johnson wrote the related but distinct “hope itself is happiness” — see the essay text ↗.

author.name: Samuel Johnson
author.heading: About Samuel Johnson
author.bio: Samuel Johnson — “Dr Johnson” — was the dominant English man of letters of the 18th century: poet, essayist, critic, and compiler of the landmark A Dictionary of the English Language (1755). His moral reflections, gathered in The Rambler and The Idler and in his letters, made him one of the most quoted writers in English, a fame cemented by James Boswell’s celebrated biography.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong
misattribution.intro: The line is authentically Johnson’s — the muddle is over where it comes from and, occasionally, which Johnson.

items.why: Johnson voiced a kindred thought in The Idler No. 58 ↗ (26 May 1759): “hope itself is happiness.” But the exact popular wording — “a species of happiness… the chief happiness which this world affords” — is from his 1762 letter, not the essay.

At least one major quote database files the line under the American statesman William Samuel Johnson rather than the English writer Samuel Johnson — a name-collision error; the words are the lexicographer’s.

misattribution.truthLine: The genuine source is Johnson’s letter of 8 June 1762, preserved in Boswell’s Life of Johnson ↗.

context.heading: The context
lead: Johnson wrote the line not as an aphorism but inside a courteous refusal. A lady had asked him to lobby the Archbishop of Canterbury to get her son into university; Johnson, unwilling to trade on influence he thought improper, delayed his reply precisely because he was reluctant to kill her hope.

His reflection turns that hesitation into a small meditation: hope is a real pleasure, perhaps the greatest life offers — which is exactly why hope indulged past reason ends in pain. The sting the modern feel-good clipping omits is the second half: “expectations improperly indulged, must end in disappointment.”
